DrFirst, INC. 
Formal Public Comment Submission 
 
 
 
2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization 
for Drugs Proposed Rule 
(CMS-0062) 
 
 
Submitted To: 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Department of Health and Human Services 
Docket ID: CMS-0062-P 
Comment Deadline: June 15, 2026 
Submitted By: 
DrFirst, Inc., www.drfirst.com 
2093 Philadelphia Pike #2334   
Clamont, DE 19703  
Date of Submission: June 15, 2026 
Colin Banas, MD, MHA, Chief Medical Officer, DrFirst, Inc. 
Tyler Wince, VP, Product & Technology, Specialty Solutions, DrFirst, Inc.

DrFirst, Inc., respectfully submits these comments in response to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services' 2026 Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule (CMS-0062), published April 10, 2026, with a public comment period closing June 15, 2026.

DrFirst is a leading healthcare technology company with more than two decades of experience in electronic prescribing, medication management, and health IT interoperability. We provide clinical decision support, electronic prior authorization (ePA), specialty pharmacy workflow, real-time prescription benefit (RTPB) tools, and formulary and benefit (F&B) data exchange to hundreds of thousands of prescribers, payers, pharmacies, and health systems nationwide. DrFirst is an ONC-certified health IT developer and an active participant in the NCPDP and HL7 standards communities.
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** DrFirst, Inc. (represented by Colin Banas, MD, MHA, Chief Medical Officer; Tyler Wince, VP Product & Technology, Specialty Solutions)
- **Stakeholder type:** Technology Vendor
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** 20+ years in electronic prescribing, medication management, and health IT interoperability; ONC-certified health IT developer; active NCPDP and HL7 community participant; operates Total Benefits platform spanning both FHIR Da Vinci (medical benefit) and NCPDP SCRIPT ePA (pharmacy benefit) in a single prescriber interface; serves hundreds of thousands of prescribers, payers, pharmacies, and health systems.

---

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

DrFirst strongly supports CMS-0062 as a genuine sea change in administrative simplification, endorsing the dual-track FHIR/NCPDP architecture, the October 1, 2027 compliance date, and the proposed centralized API endpoint directory. The company urges CMS to eliminate or materially sunset the Direct Data Entry (portal) exception, designate the CRD Coverage Information extension as the authoritative mechanism for medical-vs.-pharmacy benefit routing, establish a joint CMS/ONC payer PA API certification program, and require clearinghouses to meet the same FHIR transition timeline as payers.

---

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, PA-DRUG-PHARMACY, FHIR-IG-REQUIRED, MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT (routing), API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING, ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE, HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS (referenced indirectly)
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 45 CFR 170.215(j) (CRD 2.2.1, DTR 2.2.0, PAS 2.2.1); CMS-0057-F (2024 PA final rule); CMS-0062-P; 89 FR 8758
- **Standards referenced:** Da Vinci CRD IG v2.2.1, DTR IG v2.2.0, PAS IG v2.2.1; NCPDP SCRIPT 2023011; NCPDP RTPB; NCPDP Formulary & Benefit (F&B); NCPDP Coverage Restriction Codes 816 and 817; ONC HTI-4 Final Rule (90 FR 37130); X12N 278

---

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Eliminating the Direct Data Entry (Portal) Exception**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED, PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Modify (strengthen)
- **Rationale:** The portal exception has been the single most powerful brake on ePA adoption—payers have no financial incentive to invest in APIs while portals satisfy compliance. "Electronic PA" currently means anything from full FHIR API automation to manual web-form data re-entry. Regence–MultiCare FHIR pilot showed PA decisions in ~2 minutes vs. days, and 71% approval rate via FHIR vs. 46% via portal. Portals cannot replicate these outcomes.
- **Specific request:** Establish a defined sunset date no later than October 1, 2028 for the DDE portal exception for all CMS-regulated payers; issue guidance clarifying that portal-based PA does not satisfy API requirements for drugs under this rule.

**Topic 2: Dual-Track FHIR/NCPDP Architecture**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, PA-DRUG-PHARMACY, MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** The distinction between medical and pharmacy benefit drugs reflects genuinely different care delivery models, prescribing workflows, and clinical contexts. FHIR Da Vinci was designed for provider-administered drugs; NCPDP SCRIPT for outpatient self-administered prescriptions. DrFirst has direct operational experience bridging both tracks through its Total Benefits platform.
- **Specific request:** Affirm the dual-track architecture as a sound and necessary regulatory position; do not collapse the two tracks into a single standard.

**Topic 3: CRD Coverage Information Extension as Authoritative Benefit-Type Routing**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify (clarify/extend)
- **Rationale:** Providers frequently do not know at point of ordering whether a drug (e.g., adalimumab, lecanemab) is covered under medical or pharmacy benefit. A meaningful percentage of specialty drug PA transactions in DrFirst's network are initially misrouted to the wrong benefit track. The CRD Coverage Information extension already supports coverage, PA requirement, and billing code signals but lacks an explicit benefit-type field.
- **Specific request:** CMS, working with HL7 and Da Vinci project, should require payers to populate a benefit-type field in CRD responses—a positive CRD response for a medical benefit drug signals the FHIR/Da Vinci track; a pharmacy benefit or null response directs to NCPDP SCRIPT workflow. Additionally, clarify that NCPDP Coverage Restriction Codes 816 and 817 should be used by PBMs in RTPB responses to signal when a drug may be covered under the medical benefit.

**Topic 4: Clearinghouse Readiness**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED, HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Approximately 162 U.S. health care clearinghouses aggregate, translate, and route electronic transactions between providers and payers—making them a critical dependency in any X12N-to-FHIR transition. CMS acknowledges uncertainty about clearinghouse FHIR adoption.
- **Specific request:** Hold clearinghouses to the same compliance timeline as payers and providers.

**Topic 5: ONC Health IT Certification for Payer-Facing APIs**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED, ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** The absence of payer-side certification is a structural asymmetry since the Meaningful Use era. ONC certification has provided rigorous implementation validation for EHR systems since 2011; no equivalent framework exists for payer technology. Without certification, compliance verification for complex FHIR IGs is impossible, undermining rule objectives.
- **Specific request:** CMS and ONC should establish a joint certification program for payer PA APIs covering CRD 2.2.1, DTR 2.2.0, and PAS 2.2.1; certification should cover conformance and real-world interoperability testing with certified EHRs; CMS should condition MA contract renewal, Medicaid MCO certification, and QHP participation on demonstrated API certification; analogous NCPDP SCRIPT ePA conformance testing should apply for pharmacy benefit drugs.

**Topic 6: API Endpoint Directory**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Absence of a centralized payer endpoint directory has been a major source of friction; vendors must discover endpoints through manual outreach, commercial directories, and bilateral negotiations—expensive, slow, and advantages large incumbents.
- **Specific request:** Require endpoints reported no later than 90 days prior to compliance deadlines; include conformance status, supported IG versions, and test environment availability; publish directory via machine-readable FHIR API (not static file) for automated discovery.

**Topic 7: October 1, 2027 Compliance Timeline**
- **Provision ID:** IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE (PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, PA-DRUG-PHARMACY)
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Da Vinci CRD, DTR, PAS IGs are mature and tested in production. NCPDP SCRIPT ePA is already deployed at scale for Medicare Part D. The primary gap is payer willingness to invest, not technical feasibility. PA burden is a daily clinical crisis—oncologists abandoning biologics, specialty pharmacy patients experiencing dangerous therapy gaps.
- **Specific request:** Hold firm against industry pressure to extend the October 2027 deadline; the 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited drug PA decision windows are minimum standards of care, not aspirational goals.

---

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1 (require vs. recommend IGs):** DrFirst strongly supports making CRD, DTR, and PAS required rather than recommended; voluntary adoption has proven insufficient to drive payer implementation.
- **S12 (technical challenges for medical benefit drug PA):** Identifies benefit-type routing (same drug, different benefit) as the primary technical challenge; recommends CRD Coverage Information extension with explicit benefit-type field as the solution.
- **S15 (medical vs. pharmacy benefit distinction):** Directly addresses the "same drug, different benefit type problem"; recommends CRD as authoritative routing mechanism and NCPDP Coverage Restriction Codes 816/817 for RTPB secondary signals.
- **S21 (timeline achievable):** Affirms October 1, 2027 is achievable for payers that engage now; Da Vinci IGs are mature and NCPDP SCRIPT ePA is already at scale for Part D.
- **S23 (API endpoint security):** Supports centralized endpoint directory; recommends machine-readable FHIR API publication format.
- **S24 (what to report for endpoints):** Recommends including conformance status, supported IG versions, and test environment availability.
- **S27 (reporting frequency):** Recommends endpoints reported no later than 90 days prior to each compliance deadline.
- **S37 (implementation challenges):** Identifies portal exception, benefit-type routing uncertainty, clearinghouse readiness, and absence of payer API certification as the four core implementation barriers.
- **S54 (testing/certification):** Strongly supports ONC certification framework extended to payer PA APIs, with real-world interoperability testing against certified EHRs as a condition of program participation.

---

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Establish a sunset date no later than October 1, 2028 for the DDE portal exception for all CMS-regulated payers.
2. Issue guidance clarifying that portal-based PA does not satisfy API requirements for drugs under this rule.
3. Affirm the dual-track FHIR Da Vinci/NCPDP SCRIPT architecture as clinically and operationally correct.
4. Work with HL7 and Da Vinci project to require payers to populate an explicit benefit-type field in CRD Coverage Information extension responses.
5. Clarify that NCPDP Coverage Restriction Codes 816 and 817 should be used by PBMs in RTPB responses to signal medical-benefit-covered drugs.
6. Hold clearinghouses to the same FHIR transition compliance timeline as payers and providers.
7. Establish a joint CMS/ONC certification program for payer PA APIs covering CRD 2.2.1, DTR 2.2.0, and PAS 2.2.1.
8. Condition MA contract renewal, Medicaid MCO certification, and QHP participation on demonstrated payer API certification.
9. Establish analogous NCPDP SCRIPT ePA conformance testing requirements for pharmacy benefit drugs.
10. Require payers to report API endpoints no later than 90 days prior to applicable compliance deadlines.
11. Require endpoint directory to include conformance status, supported IG versions, and test environment availability.
12. Publish the endpoint directory via machine-readable FHIR API rather than a static file.
13. Hold firm against pressure to extend the October 1, 2027 compliance deadline.

---

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Portal exception blocking true ePA interoperability; benefit-type routing ambiguity causing misrouted PA transactions; absence of payer API certification creating unverifiable compliance; clearinghouse readiness as an unaddressed dependency.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Without portal sunset, payers have no incentive to invest in APIs; without benefit-type routing resolution, duplicate PA submissions, delays, and denials based on wrong workflow will continue; without certification, compliance verification gap will undermine rule objectives.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Payer willingness to invest (not technical feasibility) is the primary gap; clearinghouse FHIR transition is unaddressed; ONC legal authority over payer certification is acknowledged as complex (but CMS programmatic authority is sufficient).

---

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** 94% of physicians report care delays tied to PA (AMA 2024); 78% report PA caused patients to abandon recommended treatments (AMA 2024); FHIR pilot PA decisions in ~2 minutes vs. days historically; 71% approval rate FHIR-based PA vs. 46% portal; 84% of CRD queries returned PA not required; approximately 162 U.S. health care clearinghouses.
- **Studies or research referenced:** AMA 2024 Prior Authorization Physician Survey; Da Vinci Project real-world pilot data (cited in CMS-0062 preamble); Regence–MultiCare FHIR pilot.
- **Examples provided:** Adalimumab and lecanemab as drugs where benefit type is ambiguous at point of ordering; oncologists abandoning biologics due to PA burden; specialty pharmacy therapy gaps from benefit-type uncertainty.

---

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Health IT vendors, payers (MA, Medicaid MCOs, QHPs), providers (especially specialists/oncologists), specialty pharmacies, clearinghouses, EHR systems, patients on specialty/biologic therapies.
- **Economic implications:** Portal sunset will require payer API investment but will reduce industry-wide connection discovery costs via centralized endpoint directory; smaller vendors will gain access to payer integrations currently cost-prohibitive.
- **Technical feasibility:** DrFirst's assessment is that October 2027 is achievable—Da Vinci IGs are mature and production-tested; NCPDP SCRIPT ePA is already deployed at scale for Part D; primary gap is payer investment willingness.
- **Patient care impact:** Portal exception perpetuates care delays; benefit-type misrouting causes duplicate submissions and denials; real-time CRD benefit-type determination would eliminate routing delays before PA initiation for specialty drug patients.

---

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive (with targeted modifications to strengthen the rule)
- **Tone:** Professional, Technical, Collaborative
- **Priority level:** High

---

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "The continued availability of the portal exception has been the single most powerful brake on ePA adoption in the U.S." — Context: Arguing for sunset of the DDE portal exception.

2. "For some payers, it means true workflow-integrated FHIR API exchange with automated coverage determinations in seconds. For others, it means a web form that a staff member opens in a separate browser tab, manually re-enters patient data, and awaits a faxed decision 3-15 business days later." — Context: Illustrating the current meaninglessness of 'electronic PA.'

3. "The primary gap is payer willingness to invest in API development ahead of a regulatory deadline, not technical feasibility." — Context: Supporting the October 2027 deadline and rejecting extension arguments.

4. "Benefit type determination should become a computable, real-time transaction that resolves before the PA request is initiated. Providers should not bear the burden of determining benefit type through manual research." — Context: Explaining why the CRD Coverage Information extension benefit-type field is essential.

---

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** — Strongly supports October 1, 2027 deadline; recommends October 1, 2028 sunset for portal exception; urges CMS to resist extension pressure.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** — Assesses Da Vinci IGs as mature and production-tested; NCPDP SCRIPT ePA already at scale; identifies payer investment willingness, not technical readiness, as the key gap.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** — References specific IG versions (CRD 2.2.1, DTR 2.2.0, PAS 2.2.1); notes IGs are well-documented and real-world tested; recommends ONC certification to validate implementation.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** — Core focus: same-drug, different-benefit-type routing problem; recommends CRD Coverage Information extension benefit-type field as authoritative resolution mechanism.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** — Portal-based PA creates manual, click-intensive burden; benefit-type misrouting generates duplicate submissions, rework, and delays.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** — PA burden causes oncologists to abandon biologics; specialty pharmacy patients experience dangerous therapy gaps from benefit-type uncertainty; 78% of physicians report patients abandoning recommended treatments due to PA.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** — Detailed analysis of DDE portal exception, X12N-to-FHIR transition, and clearinghouse role in current PA transaction routing.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** — Recommends CMS work with HL7, Da Vinci project, NCPDP, ONC, and clearinghouses to resolve benefit-type routing and implement certification framework.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** — Centralized endpoint directory with machine-readable FHIR API publication will create public compliance accountability and reduce vendor discovery friction.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** — Extensive analysis of how portal exception disadvantages innovative vendors vs. incumbents; how certification would level the technical quality playing field; clearinghouse role as critical dependency.
